prize_parts.citation: For showing that liquid-liquid phase separation of multivalent biomolecules organises the living cell into membraneless compartments.

statement.case_for: Biomolecular phase separation imported a classical physical-chemical idea, demixing governed by multivalency, concentration and interfacial thermodynamics, into the organisation of the cell. The 2009 P-granule observation by Hyman and Brangwynne and the multivalent-interaction phase diagrams of Rosen supply both the founding observation and the quantitative framework. The concept has been reproduced across many laboratories for over fifteen years, redirected research on neurodegeneration and RNA biology, and given synthetic chemists a design principle for compartments without membranes. It is the clearest case on the shortlist of a new concept of molecular organisation rather than a new tool or reaction.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the concept is still being contested at its edges: which in-cell assemblies are genuine equilibrium phases, whether condensate formation is functional or incidental, and how many in vitro demonstrations are artefacts of overexpression or crowding. A prize that endorsed the concept too broadly could age badly. There is also a real question of whether this is chemistry or cell biology, and a three-name cut necessarily excludes Pappu and Mittag, whose sequence-grammar and theory work is physical-chemical in the strict sense. Compared with B017, the maturity and the demonstrated consequences are plainly less settled.

responses.point: Aili ranks massively parallel sequencing first as chemistry enabling nearly all of modern biomedicine, mature and overdue, with a clean core claim in the Balasubramanian and Klenerman Solexa chemistry, and places condensates fourth with a doubt on whether they belong in Chemistry.
responses.response: I accept that B017 is stronger than B029 on maturity and on demonstrated consequence, and I would not oppose it, so I keep it as my first alternative. I disagree on the chemistry-versus-biology worry for condensates: the explanatory content is phase behaviour, valence and interfacial thermodynamics, which is physical chemistry. The sequencing case needs the same scrutiny, since Sanger sequencing was recognised in 1980 and the committee must decide whether this is a new chemical principle or a scaling of known nucleotide chemistry. I also doubt that a two-name Balasubramanian and Klenerman prize can be defended without leaving out Mayer and Ju.

responses.point: Linke, as chair, places halide perovskites first for a clear physical principle and large generative potential, accepting that stability and credit among six groups remain unresolved, and puts sequencing second.
responses.response: I agree that perovskites have a clear principle and extraordinary speed of impact, but I find the case less mature than he does. The central question for a prize is whether the absorber class will have lasting consequences, and operational stability, lead toxicity and a three-way priority dispute between Miyasaka, Park and Snaith are all open. I would put condensates ahead on the stability of the underlying principle, even though the in vivo debate is real, whereas the perovskite debate concerns whether the technology works at scale. I would be glad to hear whether he sees stability as a reason to wait or just a reason to word the citation carefully.

responses.point: Aqvist backs sequencing, Pd C-N coupling and the Car-Parrinello method, ranks energy-landscape theory seventh, and does not rank condensates; he judges perovskites premature and wants game-changing consequences.
responses.response: I share his scepticism about perovskite maturity. On condensates I would argue that the consequence is conceptual, since a generation of cell biology and neurodegeneration work is framed in terms of phase separation, but I concede it is harder to point to a deployed technology than for sequencing or Pd amination. On energy-landscape theory I agree with his ranking: the funnel is an organising principle with a distributed credit set (Wolynes, Onuchic, Dill, Fersht), and the 2024 prize has altered the context. For me that places B037 below B029.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks nitrogenase first as a mechanism-in-living-systems problem, with structure from Rees and Einsle, genetics from Dean and Ribbe and kinetics from Seefeldt, and cautions that the N2 reduction mechanism is still debated.
responses.response: I find the nitrogenase case scientifically compelling and mature in its structural results, but the same reservation applies as for condensates: the final mechanistic story is unfinished, and with five credited people and three structure, genetics and mechanism strands the allocation is at least as hard as for B029. If the committee weighs mechanistic rigour over conceptual reach, I would want to hear how he would phrase a citation that does not overclaim the mechanism. I do not rank it above sequencing on the evidence in the opening ballots.

uncertainties: How strongly the in vivo evidence for liquid-like condensates will be weighted given continuing criticism of artefacts and of overexpression.
Whether the committee accepts a three-person cut that omits Pappu and Mittag, or prefers a narrower claim around the founding observation.
Whether sequencing (B017) can be given a defensible laureate set, given the Solexa, 454 and terminator-chemistry lineages.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B029. For B067 my research on lipid self-assembly and membranes is close to the underlying science and I would flag that proximity, although I have no personal or institutional link to the named candidates. I sit with Lund colleagues Linke and Somfai, which is not a conflict for these candidates.
